title: Find a silent toilet leak in ten minutes
summary: A running toilet can waste a bathtub a day. Food coloring in the tank tells you in ten minutes whether yours is leaking.
body:
Put food coloring in the tank, wait ten minutes without flushing, and look in the bowl (story-standard test). Color in the bowl means the flapper is passing water — a part most hardware stores stock for a few dollars.

If two toilets leak, the story math at tier-1 prices is roughly $9–14 a month — small, but it never sleeps.

title: Read your own meter (and catch leaks before the bill)
summary: Three numbers, once a week, same time: the fastest way to know if water is moving when nothing is running.
body:
Read the dial Friday evening and Saturday morning before any use (story method). If it moved overnight and nothing ran, something is leaking or a toilet is cycling.

The district's story re-read policy is kinder when you catch it in the first cycle — another reason the meter lid is worth lifting.

title: Water the yard like the Ossel River is low — because in August it is
summary: Deep and infrequent beats daily sprinkles: roots, timing before 9am, and why tier-3 pricing exists.
body:
One deep soak a week (story guidance for Carrow Bend soils) grows deeper roots than daily light watering. Water before 9am so less evaporates, and keep sprinklers off pavement.

This is also the honest reason for tier 3: peak August pumping sizes the system. Shaving peak use is the cheapest 'new supply' the district has.

title: Winterize: the two pipes that actually freeze in Carrow Bend
summary: Hose bibs and the crawl-space run on the north wall. Fifteen minutes in October beats a January main-break call at your house.
body:
Disconnect hoses, shut the interior hose-bib valves, and insulate the north-wall crawl-space run (story checklist from local break calls). Leave cabinet doors open on the coldest nights if that run serves a sink.

If a pipe does freeze, shut the house valve first — its location is worth knowing before you need it.
